title: Hunkenr Folding Saw Review: Better Than Nothing
content:
The long and luxurious Silky Katanaboy is the Cadillac Fleetwood of folding saws, but it ain’t cheap. Travis found a more economical option in the 500 mm Hunkenr folding saw, but he’s a little conflicted about it.

Trail work usually addresses one of three problems: Erosion, overgrowth, or downed trees. Fixing erosion and overgrowth is slow. A project can stretch for miles, and one person might take an hour to restore just 50 feet. Downed trees are different. Each one may only take up a couple yards, but they’re often spread out across an entire trail. Just a few quick cuts might liberate the whole thing. I usually do those cuts with a chainsaw. But not always.

There are times of year when some (or all) of our forest is off-limits to chainsaws due to high fire danger. But in California, most saw projects pop up in the wet season anyway. The heavy rain and high-elevation snow provide us with plenty of newly fallen trees, and we’re assured there will be no fire restrictions. But sometimes there’s just one lonely piece of deadfall out in the middle of nowhere, or in the middle of summer. That’s when I use a handsaw.

Let’s pause for a quick saw sidebar. Every land manager is different, but in the US National Forest, anyone cutting wood over 5” in diameter with any tool is supposed to be certified. I know we’re all adults here, but rogue trailbuilding – even rogue trail maintaining – may have consequences. More importantly, it may be unnecessary. You’ve probably got a nearby organization of hikers and/or mountain bikers that needs volunteers. It’s legal, and more importantly, it’s efficient. Many hands make light work. With that out of the way, let’s move on.

Photos: Silky

Short of your great-great-grandpa’s two-person saw, the gold standard for non-motorized big cuts is the Silky Katanaboy. Silky saws work at almost supernatural speeds. I carry a Silky Pocketboy on most rides, and I use it pretty regularly. It’s quick to deploy, cut, and stow. And I can’t find another folding saw with the same curved blade and compact form. Even if I could, I’d still run the Pocketboy. It’s only $60. A Katanaboy, on the other hand, starts at $280.

I recognize there’s a hint of hypocrisy here. It’s pretty rich that a guy who runs a $600 seatpost would balk at a $280 saw. But I use that seatpost hundreds of times a ride. I may only use a large folding saw a few times a year. If chainsaws weren’t an option for our trail organization, I’d probably own a Katanaboy Professional, which goes for $460. But I needed something much cheaper to justify the purchase. And I found it in the Hunkenr 500 mm Folding Saw.

Ok, second sidebar. I keep my Amazon shopping to a minimum. Same with my driving or my consumption of single-use plastics. But sometimes there is just no other reasonable choice. Amazon is the only place this saw is sold. Sure, other retailers sell cheap, large folding saws. But none are as big, or have as long a handle as the Hunkenr saw. There’s a reason this is such a coveted configuration. Not only does it provide an extended stroke for speedier cuts of larger logs; it’s also safer. I’m farther from danger when gravity takes over, and I’ve got a two-step head start if I need to run.

These similarities to the Katanaboy leave me feeling more icky than the Amazon thing. Silky designed a phenomenal saw, and the Hunkenr is effectively IP theft. Theft that I supported by buying it, and am supporting further by writing positively about it. My justification is that I’m using this saw to improve public trails on a volunteer basis (even though I’m not doing it for you). And I assume anyone reading this would be doing the same. So, I’ll say this: If you can afford a Katanaboy, buy one. I’ve used one long enough to say that you won’t be disappointed. But if you can’t afford one, the Hunkner saw will perform enough Good Works to atone for its sins.

Hunkener 500 mm Folding Saw Quick Hits

  • 520 mm blade (480 mm of teeth)
  • 660 mm total length when folded
  • 1,160 mm total length when open
  • 5 teeth per 30 mm
  • 988 g
  • SK5-grade steel
  • Two locking positions (fully open and fully closed)
  • No replacement blades available
  • Teeth can be sharpened
  • $64.88

Carrying the Hunkenr Saw

Even when stowed, the Hunkenr saw is big. It outsizes my tallest backpack by 130 mm. It includes a sheath with a shoulder strap, but that doesn’t help me when I’m wearing a pack. So, my preferred portage method is to strap the saw below my downtube. This is on a size XL frame, but it actually fits nearly as well on my wife’s size small. Ride carefully if it extends below your bottom bracket, but it’s unlikely to extend below your chainring. And if the downtube is not an option for any reason, I had no leg-clearance issues strapping it alongside my top tube.

The sheath has a longitudinal divider, which creates a perfect chamber for me to insert a piece of old sleeping pad that protects my downtube. Two small Voile-style straps are plenty to keep it secure. I don’t even notice it down there. I’ve carried this saw on a few 20-mile+ rides that were 10% business and 90% party. The whole point of having this kind of saw is to tackle remote projects. So, you might as well have some fun getting there and back.

Why Not Use a Pocket Chainsaw?

Of course, you could skip all this by using a pocket chainsaw like the one John reviewed. They can cut just as big, and with a tiny fraction of the weight and bulk. They make perfect sense for some projects, but they have their disadvantages. Most notably, they’re thick.

The teeth have to be wide enough to clear the chain itself. My pocket chainsaw is a little under 5mm wide. That’s more than twice as thick as the 1.7mm Hunkenr blade. So, you have to remove more than twice the material. Maybe not a big deal if you’ve got one item on your to-do list. But the math shifts if you’ve got three or four. Also, you have to work very close to the log with a pocket chainsaw. Sometimes even straddling it, which can go wrong in a hurry if things slide or fall in a way you didn’t expect. You have more options in where and how to approach a cut with a folding saw.

Hunkenr Saw Design

The locking mechanism will be familiar to those who’ve used any Silky saw. A stiff metal spring-loaded latch fixes it in the open position, but these bigger saws have a few extra perks. Gomboys and Pocketboys don’t have a notch to lock them into the “closed” position, but the Katanaboy and Hunkenr do. There’s also a knob to lock the latch in place. It’s a bit of a faff to do every time you deploy the saw, and would probably vibrate out if you skip it. But it’s worth the peace of mind. The hinge itself is also pretty stout, with a lot of surface-area contact and no wobble. I’d just recommend adding some blue Loc-Tite to the pivot bolt.

And I’d call the handle itself “confidence-inspiring.” The rubber is very well affixed to the aluminum core. It’s not like a chainstay protector that’s already peeling at the corners on your first ride. It’s part of the saw. And it’s a nice perk that the core is aluminum. The hinge junction is steel, and it’d probably have been cheaper to make the whole thing from one material. But I appreciate that they went to the trouble of riveting in a lighter handle. That saves a lot of weight on something this big.

Using the Hunkenr Saw

Again, that size is why this style of saw is so beloved. I already mentioned its safety benefit. I’d argue a hand saw can be more dangerous than a chainsaw because you’re close to the hazard for a longer time, always jiggling it back and forth. Yes, these saws only cut on the “pull” stroke, but there’s still constant loading and unloading that can eventually help send a precarious log or surrounding debris tumbling. Holding the bottom of the handle with one hand and finishing a cut from a distance is a perfectly effective way to use the Hunkenr saw. Up until then, the long handle makes it easy to use two hands, and switch your grip in multiple ways throughout a cut to minimize fatigue.

And it is fatiguing. Cutting through a 12” log will take a while. There are too many variables in wood type for me to offer a comprehensive breakdown of how long a given cut will take, but I’ve had a few thick dry guys fight me for 15 minutes, including a rest or two. It helps to get comfortable if you know you’re in a safe position. And I generally use just the weight of my forward resting arm to provide the downward force. The key to making an efficient cut isn’t to force it, but to maintain long, straight strokes. I treat each log like a long climb. You just have to be patient.

You also have to strategize. On top of planning out how to remove an obstruction with the fewest cuts, you have to “read the binds.” That is, anticipate if and where the log is going to pinch your saw once you start to remove material. Binding isn’t usually a big issue when using a handsaw because you’re probably just clearing brush. But a bind can helplessly trap your saw on heavy limbs.

That’s why I carry wedges, though you need the right kind. Some wedges are meant for the wide gap (or “kerf”) left by a chainsaw. For a folding saw, I use the Forester Mini Wedges … but not when I shot the action photos for this review. The night before I hit the trail, my Mini Wedges were nowhere to be found. I had to use the skinniest full-sized wedge I had on hand. Two days later, I found my Mini Wedges in my bikepacking bike’s frame bag. Hope you enjoyed that little peek behind the curtain!

The other thing I plan for is dirt and rocks. I’ll abuse my little $25 Ace Hardware saw all day long. It usually cuts thin, green stalks that are usually close to the ground. But the Hunkenr saw needs to stay sharp, so I keep it out of the dirt. It’s not good for flush-cutting low, thin chaparral anyway. You can’t steady a branch with one hand and saw it with the other. It’s for thick wood, and nothing else. So, if I’m working close to the ground, I check the area surrounding the cut and dig a deep trench below it if necessary. I’m very methodical with it. It’s a bit of a pain, but I don’t use it often. It’s worth the extra time to make sure it lasts. Plus, I don’t want to have to buy another one.

Pros:

  • Cheap
  • Fast
  • Portable
  • Sharpenable
  • Robust construction
  • Long handle decreases fatigue and increases safety

Cons:

  • Replacement blades aren’t available
  • Only sold on Amazon
